title: A stranger paid for my gas at a truck stop. Six hours later, I saw his face on the evening news — and the police were asking everyone to find him (PART 2)

blocks.text: …has a dashcam. And he may have told her exactly where that family is."
I grabbed my phone and called the number on the screen. My hands were shaking so badly I misdialed twice.

A detective called me back within minutes. I told him everything: the declined card, the forty-seven dollars, the man's warning to avoid Exit 214 because of an accident. There was a long silence on the line. Then he said, "Ma'am, there was no accident reported at 214."

The missing family, the Garcias, a couple and their two young daughters, had been driving home from a wedding the night before. Their car never arrived. Searchers had been combing a stretch of Interstate 70 forty miles west, where their phone last pinged a tower. Exit 214 wasn't even on their map.
Within the hour, a state trooper found fresh tire marks leading off the shoulder just past Exit 214.

The Garcias' car was at the bottom of a wooded ravine, invisible from the road. All four of them were alive. The father had a broken leg, the mother a concussion. The girls were cold and terrified but unhurt. They'd been trapped for almost nine hours.

The man from the truck stop turned himself in to a sheriff's office that afternoon, after a friend called him about the news. His name was Earl Simmons, a long-haul trucker. He'd seen headlights go off the road ahead of him and pulled over, but he couldn't see the car in the dark, and his phone had no signal. He drove twelve miles to the truck stop and asked the young cashier to call 911. The cashier, flustered and new to the job, gave the dispatcher the wrong mile marker.
Then Earl had a delivery deadline and kept driving, believing help was on the way.
The police had wanted him as a witness, not a suspect. The news report made it sound otherwise.
My dashcam had recorded the whole conversation at the pump, including Earl pointing toward the road and saying "214." The detective said that clip is what convinced them to move the search.

I met Earl and the Garcias at a hospital in Kansas City a week later. The girls gave him a card that said "Thank you for paying it forward." I finally paid him back his forty-seven dollars. He put it straight into the girls' piggy bank.
